guide.title: Neurological Emergencies
guide.lead: In stroke, time is brain: find the deficit, record when they were last known well, check the glucose and go to the right stroke centre. In seizures, protect the patient, time the seizure and treat when it reaches 5 minutes.

sections.title: BE-FAST
rows: Sudden loss of balance or coordination
Sudden vision loss or double vision
When were they last known well?

steps.title: Glucose
steps.text: Low glucose mimics stroke: treat it first (5.3).

steps.title: Last known well
steps.text: Exact time. Thrombolysis up to 4.5 hours; thrombectomy for large-vessel occlusion up to 24 hours in selected patients.

steps.title: Leave the BP alone
steps.text: Don't lower it in the field.

steps.title: Destination
steps.text: Stroke centre; thrombectomy-capable centre for suspected large-vessel occlusion per protocol. Pre-notify.

sections.title: Seizures

steps.text: Protect the head; move hazards; time it.
Nothing in the mouth; don't restrain.
Midazolam 10 mg IM (over 40 kg) or 5 mg IM (13–40 kg), or buccal/intranasal per protocol.

sections.after: Afterwards: recovery position, look for injury, transport if it's a first seizure, injury, pregnancy, diabetes or no return to baseline.

groups.title: Thunderclap headache
items: Worst ever, peaks within a minute

groups.title: Meningitis
items: Fever, stiff neck, headache, photophobia, confusion

quiz.q: The Cincinnati Prehospital Stroke Scale checks:
options: Facial droop, arm drift and speech

quiz.q: Continuous jerking of all four limbs for 6 minutes:
quiz.explanation: 5 minutes or more: treat with a benzodiazepine.

quiz.q: Slurred speech and right arm weakness with glucose 48 mg/dL resolve completely after glucose. This was:
options: A stroke that resolved by chance
quiz.explanation: Always check glucose in stroke-like symptoms.

quiz.q: The most important time to document in suspected stroke:
options: When the patient was last known well
When symptoms were first noticed by a stranger
quiz.explanation: It decides thrombolysis and thrombectomy eligibility.

quiz.q: Thrombolysis for ischemic stroke is possible up to:
quiz.explanation: Thrombectomy for large-vessel occlusion can extend to 24 hours in selected patients.

quiz.q: IM midazolam for status epilepticus in a 70 kg adult:
During a tonic-clonic seizure you should:
options: Protect the head and time the seizure
quiz.explanation: Nothing in the mouth; no restraint.

quiz.q: "Worst headache of my life", peaking within a minute, suggests:
quiz.explanation: A thunderclap headache is a neurological emergency.

quiz.q: Fever, stiff neck and a non-blanching rash. Precautions?
options: Droplet: mask yourself and the patient

flashcards.question: Ischemic vs hemorrhagic stroke
flashcards.answer: Ischemic (about 87%): a clot blocks an artery. Hemorrhagic: a vessel bursts; often sudden severe headache, vomiting and rapid decline.

flashcards.question: BE-FAST
flashcards.answer: Balance, Eyes, Face, Arm, Speech, Time. Balance and eyes catch posterior strokes.

flashcards.question: Phases of a tonic-clonic seizure
flashcards.answer: Tonic (stiffening, loss of consciousness), clonic (rhythmic jerking, incontinence, tongue biting), postictal (confusion, drowsiness).

flashcards.question: Status epilepticus
flashcards.answer: A seizure lasting 5 minutes or more, or repeated seizures without recovery between. Treat with a benzodiazepine.

flashcards.question: Seizure dos and don'ts
flashcards.answer: Do: protect the head, time it, loosen clothing, stay. Don't: restrain, put anything in the mouth, give anything to drink.

flashcards.question: AEIOU-TIPS
flashcards.answer: Alcohol, Epilepsy/electrolytes, Insulin, Overdose/Oxygen, Uremia, Trauma/Temperature, Infection, Psychiatric/Poisoning, Stroke/Shock.

flashcards.question: Signs of bacterial meningitis
flashcards.answer: Fever, stiff neck, severe headache, confusion, photophobia; a non-blanching rash suggests meningococcal sepsis. Droplet precautions.

flashcards.question: Unconscious hypoglycemic patient
flashcards.answer: Airway first; glucagon IM or IV dextrose (ALS); recovery position; never oral glucose.

critical.scenario: A 72-year-old was fine at breakfast 2 hours ago. Now: slurred speech, left facial droop, can't lift the left arm. Glucose 112 mg/dL.
critical.question: Diagnosis and critical information?

options.t: Acute stroke: record last known well (2 hours ago), BE-FAST, oxygen only if SpO₂ below 94%, rapid transport to a stroke centre with pre-notification

options.f: Arm weakness and speech problems rule that out.
Leave BP alone in the field.

options.t: Wait to see if it resolves

critical.explanation: She's within 4.5 hours for thrombolysis; screen for large-vessel occlusion per protocol.

critical.scenario: A 30-year-old had a 3-minute generalized seizure at work, his first ever. Now confused and drowsy, bitten tongue, stable vital signs, glucose 96 mg/dL.
critical.question: Priorities?

options.t: Monitor airway and mental status, recovery position, check injuries, transport for evaluation
options.f: Correct: a first seizure needs a cause found.

critical.explanation: Causes include bleeding, tumour, infection and metabolic problems.

critical.scenario: A 19-year-old student has fever 39.6 °C, vomiting, severe headache and can't touch chin to chest. A non-blanching purple rash on her legs.
critical.question: Diagnosis and precautions?

options.t: Bacterial (meningococcal) meningitis: mask the patient and yourself, oxygen, rapid transport and pre-alert

options.f: A non-blanching rash is an emergency.
Fever and rash rule that out.

critical.explanation: She needs antibiotics urgently; give them per protocol if your service carries them.
